spoken: At three thousand revolutions a minute, a car engine's crankshaft turns fifty times a second.
Yet each cylinder burns its fuel only twenty-five times a second, which is once every two turns.
Its piston makes four trips for every burn, and only one of them pushes.
This is the four-stroke cycle. It was first patented by a man who never built one,
and made to work by a former grocery salesman, who later lost his patent.
Let's open one up. This is a simplified diagram of a single cylinder.
Inside the cylinder, a piston slides up and down.
A connecting rod links the piston to the crankshaft, which turns.
At the top, there are two valves. One lets air and fuel in, and the other lets burnt gas out.
Cams on a camshaft push them open, and springs close them again.
Between them sits the spark plug.
The piston's highest point is top dead centre, and its lowest is bottom dead centre.
One trip between them, up or down, is a stroke.
As the crank turns, the piston follows, but not in a perfectly even rhythm.
After a quarter turn, the piston has already covered more than half its stroke.
The tilting rod makes it hurry through the top half of the stroke, and dawdle through the bottom.
Now let's run one cycle, slowly, from the top.
Stroke one is intake. The intake valve opens, and the falling piston draws in air and fuel.
Stroke two is compression. Both valves close, and the rising piston squeezes the mixture into about a tenth of the space.
By now the crankshaft has turned once, all the way round.
Near the top, the spark plug fires, and the mixture starts to burn.
Stroke three is power. The hot, high-pressure gas drives the piston down.
This is the only stroke that pushes on the crank.
Stroke four is exhaust. The exhaust valve opens, and the rising piston pushes the burnt gas out.
Then it all starts again. That's four strokes, two turns of the crank, and one push.
The camshaft turns at half the crankshaft's speed, so each valve opens once per cycle.
What carries the piston through the three strokes that don't push? It's a heavy flywheel.
It soaks up energy from each power stroke, and gives some back to squeeze the next charge.
The idea is older than the engine that made it famous.
In eighteen sixty, Étienne Lenoir, in Paris, built a gas engine that burned its fuel without compressing it first.
It turned only about four percent of the fuel's energy into work.
A travelling salesman in Germany, Nicolaus Otto, learned of it, and started building engines himself.
In eighteen sixty-two he tried one that compressed its charge first. It ran for a few minutes, then destroyed itself.
That same year, in France, Alphonse Beau de Rochas patented the four-stroke cycle. But he never built an engine.
In eighteen sixty-four, Otto and Eugen Langen founded the first company devoted to making engines.
Their atmospheric engine, at about twelve percent efficiency, won a gold medal at the Paris World's Fair of eighteen sixty-seven.
Then, in eighteen seventy-six, Otto's company built an engine that compressed its charge in four strokes.
It was an immediate success, and the first commercially successful engine to compress its charge in the cylinder.
Two of Otto's former engineers, Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, made it small and fast enough for vehicles.
But in eighteen eighty-six the patent was cancelled in Germany, because Beau de Rochas had patented the cycle first.
By eighteen eighty-nine, more than fifty companies were building Otto-type engines.
And the cycle still carries his name. It's called the Otto cycle.
Why does squeezing first help so much? Engineers answer with a graph of pressure against volume.
This is the idealised version, the Otto cycle, traced as our engine turns.
During intake, the volume grows, at about the pressure outside.
During compression, the volume shrinks tenfold, and the pressure climbs steeply.
Combustion is treated as instant, at the top, so the pressure leaps while the volume stays the same.
During the power stroke, the hot gas expands and pushes, and its pressure falls.
At the bottom, the exhaust valve opens and the pressure drops back.
During exhaust, the piston sweeps the gas out, and the loop closes.
The area inside the loop is the net work, which is what the power stroke gave, minus what the compression cost.
The compression ratio is the cylinder's largest volume divided by its smallest.
In the ideal cycle, the efficiency depends on that ratio alone.
The efficiency is one, minus the ratio to the power of one minus gamma, where gamma is one point four for air.
Squeeze four to one, and the ideal engine turns forty-three percent of its heat into work.
At ten to one, it's sixty percent, and at sixteen to one, it's sixty-seven percent.
Real engines lose energy to heat and friction along the way. A petrol engine turns about thirty percent into useful work.
But the lesson holds. If you squeeze harder, you get more work from the same fuel.
So why do most petrol car engines stop at around eight to twelve to one?
Squeezing a gas heats it, and a hot enough mixture can ignite by itself.
Normally, the spark starts a flame front that sweeps across the chamber.
But if the unburnt mixture ahead of the flame gets too hot, pockets of it explode all at once.
That's called knock. It causes a metallic pinging, and pressure spikes that can damage the engine.
A fuel's octane rating measures how well it resists igniting by itself. Higher octane allows more squeeze.
And modern engines listen for knock with sensors, and fire the spark later when they hear it.
So far, everything happened exactly at the top or bottom of a stroke. Real engines don't wait.
The spark fires early, at some ten to forty degrees of crank rotation before the top.
The flame takes time to burn, and the peak pressure should come just after the top.
The flame doesn't speed up with the engine, so at higher revs the spark needs a longer head start.
The valves are early, too. They open before the end of a stroke, and close after it.
At the end of the exhaust stroke, both valves are briefly open at once. This is called valve overlap.
The outgoing exhaust is moving fast, and it helps draw the fresh charge in behind it.
Designers aim to close the exhaust valve just as the fresh charge reaches it.
Racing engines use lots of overlap. Road engines, which must idle smoothly below a thousand revolutions a minute, use less.
Many now shift their camshafts as they run, to get both power at high revs and a smooth idle.
One cylinder gives one push every two turns. That's a lumpy way to drive a car.
So most car engines have several cylinders on one crankshaft, firing in turn.
Spaced evenly, the power strokes come every seven hundred and twenty degrees, divided by the number of cylinders.
With four cylinders, that's every hundred and eighty degrees, which gives a push every half turn.
A straight four usually fires its cylinders in the order one, three, four, two.
Here is the twisting force that the gas puts on the crank, in an idealised model.
One cylinder gives one big shove, then a long wait, with a drag while it compresses.
Four cylinders give one shove after another.
With six cylinders, the power strokes overlap, and the push is smoother still.
Even spacing means less vibration and a smoother sound.
There is another way to light the fire, with no spark at all.
A diesel draws in only air, and squeezes it much harder, typically fifteen to twenty-three to one.
Squeezing air that hard heats it by hundreds of degrees.
Near the top, fuel is sprayed in, and it ignites in the hot air by itself.
With no fuel in the cylinder during the squeeze, nothing can ignite early, so a diesel can squeeze harder.
That's one reason diesels are efficient. Big, slow ship diesels reach up to fifty-five percent.
And instead of throttling its air, a diesel sets its power by how much fuel it injects.
Rudolf Diesel's first prototype fired in eighteen ninety-three, and his third, tested in eighteen ninety-seven, turned about twenty-six percent of its fuel into work.
And it runs the same four strokes of intake, compression, power and exhaust.
So here is the whole idea.
Draw in, squeeze, burn and push out. That's four strokes, in two turns of the crank.
The squeeze makes it efficient, and knock sets the limit on the squeeze.
Patented in eighteen sixty-two by a man who never built one, and made to work by Otto in eighteen seventy-six,
it is still the cycle inside most car engines.
At three thousand revolutions a minute, that's two turns and one push, twenty-five times every second.
